# Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta (MN 114 (PTS MN iii 45))

**ID:** MN 114 (PTS MN iii 45)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated
**PTS:** MN iii 45
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn114
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta* ("What Should and Should Not Be Cultivated", MN 114) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha introduces a brief thematic outline on what things are to be cultivated or used (*sevitabba*) and what are not (*asevitabba*), which Venerable Sāriputta then undertakes to elaborate in full detail [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Gaffney 2003; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The fundamental governing criterion is ethical and psychological: conduct or states that cause unwholesome qualities (*akusalā dhammā*) to increase and wholesome qualities (*kusalā dhammā*) to diminish are to be avoided, whereas those that cause unwholesome states to decrease and wholesome states to increase are to be cultivated [Dhammanan 2007; Nance 2004; Rogell 2003; Wen 2011].

Sāriputta systematically applies this evaluative principle to threefold action in bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, as well as to mental attitudes, views, the objects of the six senses, and the monastic requisites [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Nance 2004]. In analyzing verbal conduct, he contrasts harsh, divisive, or frivolous speech with gentle, reconciling, and timely speech [Dhammanan 2007; Nance 2004]. Under bodily and mental action, the text details the ten skilful courses of action, including the avoidance of sexual misconduct with protected women and the abandonment of covetousness (*abhijjā*), malevolence, and wrong view [Gnanarama 1998; Bluck 2006; Webster 2005].

In early canonical cross-referencing, the sutta is mentioned in the *Cullaniddesa* (Cnd 22), the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 7, Mnd 14), and the *Puggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.3) [SuttaCentral]. According to SuttaCentral, full parallels include AN 10.54, AN 9.6, AN 3.28, MN 41 (*Sāleyyaka Sutta*), and the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* discourse MĀ 109, with partial parallels in EĀ 45.3, MĀ 107–108, Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 73), and MN 17 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reports widespread Pali-internal text reuse, sharing its largest segments with AN 10, DN 21 (*Sakkapañha Sutta*), AN 9, AN 4, MN 70, AN 3, and MN 41 [DharmaNexus]. Its evaluative framework directly parallels that found in DN 21 [DharmaNexus; Wen 2011]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text cross-linguistically with the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (ZH_T01_0026, agreeing with SuttaCentral), the *Dīrgha Āgama* (ZH_T01_0001), the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and various Tibetan canonical texts [DharmaNexus].
